We also got a DSL line. That was an exciting leap. I inherited the P1 and installed Windows ME on it (because newer) and overclocked to 200MHz using a jumper on the motherboard. Hey!

I began doing this around a year ago, when I rooted my Android phone and installed Cyanogenmod, a variant of Android which has an emphasis on privacy.

Have a look at this list of privacy-conscious email providers.

Basically, if an online service is free to use, you are the product. Your data is being used and sold. Start paying for the services you use online. I have used KolabNow and Posteo.

  • KolabNow.com (formerly mykolab.com) costs $60/year for for a email-only account or $120 per year for the full group collaboration suite. It is hosted in Switzerland, where privacy laws are pretty solid. You can add your own domains to it as long as you own that domain (blah@hurpdy.blah). It doesn't say much about the duration of their logs.

  • Posteo.de costs $13/year. It is hosted in Germany. Posteo has a more Gmail-like offering, and will not allow you to add your own domain. It holds logs for 7 days.

I held an account with both sites for a while but found that I preferred Posteo. I'm happy with the level of privacy they offer.

I found Duck Duck Go's search capabilities on par with startpage's. I also like how, if DDG can't find something, you can choose to instead search google via DDG just like startpage would by adding "!g" to the start of your search term. So, searching for "cars" and choosing to reroute to google, you'd search "!g cars".

Also check out Prism Break. It lists popular proprietary software and software-as-a-service (SAAS) and their open source, privacy-conscious alternative.

I'm a Fallout fan. I own Fallout 1, 2, Tactics, 3, and New Vegas, as well as much of the DLC.

So I heard that there's a new fallout game coming out.

I have one problem: It isn't out. It won't be out for a long time. Why are they wasting my time telling me about it now?

To me, a game announcement in 2015 should go like this: "Fallout 4 is coming -- It'll be available on the Steam store at the end of this announcement!"

This idea of releasing something without much notice isn't without precedent. Beyonce released a new self-titled album on iTunes in 2013 without any prior notice -- it debuted at #1. It broke her own sales records, and iTunes sales records.

From where I'm standing, there's no benefit to this long lag between announcement and release. When I discovered there was a new game, I had my credit card in hand, and I was ready to order that second -- but there's nothing to order. Who knows if I'll be that excited when the game actually comes out at some point? Perhaps I'll have moved on to another interest by then.

Now, some people might suggest that it's beneficial for the company to ramp up the hype machine before release, to get people wanting to buy the game. I disagree with this idea. It's more beneficial for the company to ramp up the hype machine at release, so people actually do buy the game.

It's frustrating for no good reason. AAA companies -- quit advertising things we can't buy. It's not winning you any sales, and it might just be losing you sales you otherwise could have gotten.
I don't like how AAA game releases are handled in 2015.

I agree. If you give me a few months between announcement and release, the excitement is pretty much gone. By that point, the chance of an impulse buy is practically 0% and I will most likely have forgotten about it or decided to wait for a sale.

Though, I guess my bank account must be happy about the pre-purchase boycott and the time to reconsider buying an expensive new game.
That is why they announce it. Why risk your entire companies reputation on people "impulse buying" your game and end up hating it? This isnt a new thing, its been this way forever.

It releases in November.

Compared to the number of AAA titles that announce games with a year or longer lead time, Fallout 4 is not bad at all.

If the game is worth getting excited about now, it'll be worth getting excited about when it releases. Unless a person is prone to impulse buying, but you can't blame Bethesda for those kinds of bad consumer habits. Some people appreciate the lead time so they can budget for it. $70 isn't a lot of money but people who live hand-to-mouth can't just rub good intentions together and make the money materialize.

Companies announcing games well ahead of launch is not new. It's been happening for many, many years. I don't think this is a "AAA games in 2015" thing. I think this is a "impatient because I can't have Fallout 4 now" thing, rationalized as a criticism of an industry that has been announcing release dates months in advance for decades.
